issues.legal_issue: A landlord may establish a bona fide personal requirement for premises to set up an independent business for a beneficiary even when the landlord did not testify, the beneficiary took other work while the case was pending, or other family members already conduct a similar business.
material_facts: The premises were sought to establish an independent family grocery business for the landlady’s son.
The son, who was also the landlady’s attorney-in-fact and the intended beneficiary, testified in support of the requirement.
The son had taken up construction contracting work after being unemployed when the suit was filed, during the long pendency of the case.
The landlady had been a partner in a grocery business, and another son operated a grocery shop independently.
issues.conclusion: The landlady bona fide required the premises to establish an independent grocery business for her son; the contrary findings of the appellate court and High Court were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 13(1)(g) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, a landlord may recover premises reasonably and bona fide required for occupation by the landlord or a person for whose benefit the premises are held. A beneficiary’s testimony may support the requirement; the landlord’s absence from the witness box does not defeat it where the beneficiary testified. Taking other work while litigation is pending does not by itself negate an intention to start the proposed business, and the existence of similar businesses conducted by other family members does not prevent the beneficiary from establishing an independent business. Section 17 provides safeguards against misuse of a decree on this ground. No earlier cases are relied on.

issues.legal_issue: A decree for eviction on the ground of bona fide personal requirement is not barred by the comparative-hardship requirement when refusing the decree would cause greater hardship to the landlord than granting it would cause to the tenant.
material_facts: The appellate court found that the landlady would suffer greater hardship if the decree were refused than the tenants would suffer if it were granted.
That finding had become final by the time the matter was considered by the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The comparative-hardship requirement was satisfied, so it did not prevent a decree for eviction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, bars a decree under Section 13(1)(g) when the court is satisfied, considering all the circumstances including the availability of other reasonable accommodation, that greater hardship would result from granting the decree than from refusing it. The final finding that refusal would cause greater hardship to the landlord satisfied this requirement. No earlier cases are relied on.
